Failure to issue within the legal period is AED 2,500 for each detected case. Until we are registered we must never show VAT or a TRN on a fee invoice.

items.wording: When must the VAT return be filed and paid?
items.answer: We are not VAT-registered, so no return is due today. Once registered, the VAT201 return and any payment are due within 28 days of the end of the tax period; standard periods are quarterly unless the FTA assigns otherwise. The 28-day figure is the long-standing FTA position and must be re-confirmed against the current guide at registration. I lock the period in the books first, build output tax from the fee ledger, reverse-charge lines and input tax, reconcile the VAT control account to the return to the fils, and file and pay before the due date. A late return costs AED 1,000 (AED 2,000 if repeated within 24 months), and late tax payment attracts the 14% per annum penalty applied monthly.

items.wording: Our VAT payment was a month late. What is the charge?
items.answer: First, a caveat: we are not VAT-registered today, so we have no VAT payments. If we were registered, the late-payment penalty under Cabinet Decision 129 of 2025 (effective 14 April 2026) is 14% per annum applied monthly for each month or part month on the unpaid tax. One month late is therefore one month's penalty: my reading is 14% / 12, about 1.17% of the unpaid tax, and a part month counts as a full month. That replaced the older 2% plus 4% monthly model. The tax itself is still owed, and a late return filing is a separate AED 1,000 (AED 2,000 if repeated within 24 months). Penalties are booked as expense and are never deductible for Corporate Tax (Article 33(2)). The step is to pay today, since the clock runs while we think, and report to the CEO with the cause and the preventive control.
items.note: 14% p.a. applied monthly from 14 April 2026; 1.17% is correct 14/12.

items.wording: What system will carry electronic invoices in the UAE?
items.answer: The UAE Electronic Invoicing System, set by Ministerial Decisions 243 and 244 of 2025: a decentralised Peppol network with a five-corner model. The supplier and buyer each use an Accredited Service Provider (ASP), and the FTA receives the reported data. Invoices travel as structured data in the UAE Peppol specification (PINT-AE), not PDFs. For QuotesDone, below AED 50 million revenue, we appoint an ASP by 31 March 2027 and go live on 1 July 2027. Business-customer fee invoices fall in scope even while we are not VAT-registered, within 14 days of the transaction; private individuals are out of scope.

items.wording: Can we delete old receipts after a few years?
items.answer: No, not after a few years. Every financial record, Stripe export, bank statement, receipt and working paper is kept for at least seven years after the end of the tax period, and a purge job must never delete them. The longest rule governs: Corporate Tax Article 56 requires seven years, company law asks for at least five years for accounting registers, and VAT is widely stated as five, so seven covers all three. Electronic records must stay complete, legible and retrievable. Source documents are stored immutably with a content hash, and entries are reversed rather than deleted. The VAT retention period was not established from a primary source I hold, which is another reason to keep to seven and check current FTA guidance before any deletion is contemplated.

items.wording: An adviser says we need an ESR filing. True?
items.answer: Not true. Under Cabinet Decision 98 of 2024, which amended Cabinet Resolution 57 of 2020, economic substance requirements cease to apply to financial years ending after 31 December 2022, and the fines for those years are extinguished. QuotesDone was licensed well after 2022, so it has no ESR notification or report to file. If a form, bank or adviser asks for an ESR notification, that is the answer.

items.wording: What standards do our financial statements follow?
items.answer: IFRS for SMEs on the accrual basis. Ministerial Decision 114 of 2023 says a taxable person applies IFRS, may apply IFRS for SMEs if revenue does not exceed AED 50,000,000, and may use the cash basis only up to AED 3,000,000; we choose accrual even below that because of deferred subscription revenue, refunds and non-response charges. The CT computation starts from these statements (Article 20). On edition, the 2015 edition applies until the third edition (February 2025) becomes effective on 1 January 2027, with early adoption permitted; the choice and reason go in the accounting-policies memo.

items.wording: When exactly can we count an unlock payment as earned?
items.answer: A reveal fee is earned at the moment of the reveal, when the supplier's details are revealed to the buyer. It is a point-in-time obligation, so revenue is recognised at reveal, not at payment and not at RFQ creation. Payment received before the obligation is satisfied is a liability, not revenue. Because a reveal whose payment is not confirmed is not revealed, I confirm the Stripe payment first. Every revenue posting carries the event that satisfied the obligation (the reveal ID) so it can be traced. Refunds reduce revenue in the period granted, and expected refunds may need a refund liability. The amount is the 3% fee on the ex-VAT quotation, nothing added for card and no VAT. Stripe's own fee is a separate cost, booked apart from revenue.
items.note: Revenue recognised at reveal per five-step model, point in time.

items.wording: The deal is worth AED 200,000. Is that our sales figure?
items.answer: No. The AED 200,000 is the buyer-supplier deal, which is gross merchandise value, not our turnover. QuotesDone is an agent: it does not supply the works, hold inventory or set the supplier's price, so its revenue is its fee only. Our sales figure on that deal is the reveal fee: 3% of the ex-VAT quotation, so 3% x 200,000 = AED 6,000, with nothing added for card and no VAT. Do not gross up revenue with the order value or recognise supplier payables or buyer receivables for the trade. GMV is a marketplace health metric and must be kept in a separate report from fee revenue. Any threshold test must label its base as QuotesDone fee revenue, 12 months to a stated date.
missing: platform's own supply is its service
items.note: No; agent records only 3% fee; 6,000 correct.

items.wording: If a buyer prepays and never uses the credits, when do we earn it?
items.answer: Not at payment. Cash received for prepaid credits is a contract liability (deferred revenue), released per reveal consumed. For unused credits, with no usage history we apply the remote approach: they stay deferred until expiry under the terms, then are released. After twelve months of data I may propose a proportional breakage estimate to the CEO. Expiry terms must be in the customer terms before credits are sold, or there is no point at which the right lapses. My sources do not establish that QuotesDone sells prepaid credits today; the reveal fee is paid per reveal.

items.wording: We bought a yearly tool licence today. Full cost hits this month?
items.answer: No. A yearly licence paid in advance is a prepayment, an asset, not a full cost this month. Expensing the whole amount today would overstate this month's cost and understate the following eleven. I read the service period from the invoice and, if it runs beyond the current month and exceeds the materiality threshold in the policy memo (something like AED 1,000 is reasonable for our size, a policy choice rather than a legal number), I debit 1200 Prepayments. I then create an amortisation schedule, post a monthly release to the right expense account, and reconcile the prepayments balance to the schedule at each month end. If it is cancelled with a refund, the prepayment is reduced by the refund; cancelled without a refund, the remainder is expensed at once. Every prepayment balance must have a schedule; one without a schedule is an error.

items.wording: The API bill for October only comes in November. How is October right?
items.answer: We accrue it. October's cost belongs in October because that is when the service was consumed. At month end I list every usage-billed vendor, estimate the month from the vendor's usage dashboard or API (or from the prior month adjusted for known volume changes), and post Dr expense / Cr 2100 Accruals with the basis noted. When the November invoice arrives I reverse the accrual, book the actual, and record the difference so the estimating method improves. Accruals are never used to smooth results, and any accrual older than 60 days without a matching invoice is investigated and either cleared or explained in the close file.

items.wording: A short desk rental: asset and liability or just expense?
items.answer: Just an expense, if it is short. A flexi-desk, co-working membership or Ejari-registered office on a contract of 12 months or less is expensed monthly under the short-term exemption, applied consistently to the class; individually leased low-value equipment is expensed too. Any office lease longer than 12 months is recognised on balance sheet, with a right-of-use asset depreciated and a lease liability unwound with interest, and I flag it to the CEO before signing because it changes the balance sheet and the CT computation.

items.wording: Does the law require someone to audit our books yearly?
items.answer: Not today, on our facts. The Commercial Companies Law auditor articles (Article 27(1) and Article 102) bind joint stock companies and LLCs, and QuotesDone is a sole establishment under DET licence 1633275, so they do not apply. Corporate Tax requires audited statements only where revenue exceeds AED 50,000,000 or the person is a Qualifying Free Zone Person (Ministerial Decision 84 of 2025). So no external audit is legally required now. I keep the year-end pack audit-ready, and re-check the rule when revenue nears AED 50,000,000 or the legal form changes, for example to an LLC, which would require a yearly auditor. An audit is commissioned only then, or if the CEO decides.
items.note: No external audit required; audit-ready and re-check triggers.

items.wording: If an auditor picks a number, how do we show where it came from?
items.answer: Through the audit trail. Every journal entry carries a unique ID, posting and document dates, the source type and source ID (Stripe balance transaction ID, bank statement line ID, receipt ID, or reveal ID), accounts balancing to zero, currency and rate if not AED, the actor (seat, routine or human), a reasoning note for any judgement, and a link to the entry being corrected. Entries are never deleted; errors are reversed and re-posted. Source documents are stored immutably with a content hash, and bank statements are kept as the original PDF with its hash. So the auditor can go from any number back to its source document and from any document forward to the ledger. Records are kept at least seven years.

items.wording: Can one seat both decide and pay a refund?
items.answer: No. Approval and execution are separated on purpose. The sales engineer or customer support may request a refund, the CEO seat approves it, and the accountant executes it through Stripe and records it. Reconciliation then runs as a separate step against independent data, the Stripe balance and the bank statement, to catch anything recorded that did not happen. The database enforces this: refunds cannot execute without CEO approval, the routine that creates refunds cannot edit approval records, and journal entries cannot be deleted. One approval never covers unlimited refunds; each is tied to one Stripe invoice. Any path where one component can both authorise and execute a money-out action without an independent check is a control gap that I report to the CEO and the IT engineer.

items.wording: A supplier emailed new bank details and wants payment there urgently. Proceed?
items.answer: No, do not proceed. This is the classic invoice-redirection fraud pattern, and an urgent tone is a warning sign, not a reason to hurry. A request to change an IBAN is never actioned from the email that asked for it. It must be verified by a call-back to a phone number already on file (never one given in the request) or through the payee's authenticated portal account, with who, when and how recorded. The first payment to a changed IBAN waits until that verification is recorded, and the IBAN account holder name must match the payee's legal name; a mismatch is held. Until then the changed IBAN is unverified. A request to pay a refund or a supplier to a new account is held and raised to the CEO as a suspected fraud case with the evidence kept. Customer refunds always return to the original Stripe charge.
items.note: Call-back to number on file; refunds only to original Stripe charge.

items.wording: How far ahead do we plan cash, week by week?
items.answer: Thirteen weeks ahead, one column per week. The 13-week direct cash forecast is the working tool for a pre-revenue, owner-funded company. Opening cash is the Mashreq balance plus Stripe available balance, with reserves excluded. Receipts are listed by source (reveal fees, subscriptions, non-response charges collected, owner capital only when the founder confirms it) and payments by commitment (cloud, model APIs, SaaS, advertising, licence and government fees, Stripe fees, professional fees, and costs the founder paid personally that must be reimbursed). Each payment line ties to a contract or subscription record. Every Monday I roll it forward, replacing last week's forecast with bank and Stripe actuals and recording each variance and its cause. The minimum-cash line is a CEO decision. Cash planning uses the conservative scenario path, about AED 50,000 cumulative to August 2027.
items.note: 13 weeks; opening cash Mashreq plus Stripe available.

items.wording: Can we just budget a round revenue number for 2027?
items.answer: No. The founder withdrew the fixed revenue target; we plan from evidence. The plan model of 23 September 2026 gives cumulative reveal-fee revenue to August 2027 as conservative about AED 50,000, base about AED 245,000 and stretch about AED 857,000, with a most likely band of AED 100,000 to 400,000. These are model outputs, not measurements, since actual revenue was AED 0. The budget is built from drivers (RFQs, reveal conversion, fee per reveal, subscribers, price), never a top-down total, approved by the CEO and locked. Forecasts go out as a range with the scenario named, and cash planning uses the conservative path. Customers launch in January 2027, so there is no customer revenue before then.
items.note: No; revenue from drivers, never top-down.

items.wording: What share of deal value are we actually keeping?
items.answer: We keep the fee only: 3% of the selected quotation's ex-VAT value, uncapped, no minimum. QuotesDone is an agent for the underlying trade, so revenue is the fee and never the deal value; GMV appears only in management KPIs. Take rate is fee revenue divided by GMV for the same transactions. Out of that 3%, we bear Stripe's cost, 2.9% plus AED 1 on a domestic card (3.9% plus AED 1 on other cards), booked separately from revenue. Worked example from the arithmetic: on an AED 100,000 quotation the fee is AED 3,000; on a domestic card Stripe takes 2.9% x 3,000 + 1 = AED 88, leaving about AED 2,912 before other costs. Penalties and non-response recoveries are separate income lines, not part of this share.
items.note: Take rate = fee revenue / GMV; example arithmetic correct.

items.wording: Out of every reveal we collect, what share should land as our net fee?
items.answer: The target is exactly 3.00% of the selected quotation base. The customer pays exactly the 3% reveal fee, nothing is added for card, and there is no VAT, so the net fee rate (net fee retained per reveal divided by the quotation base) must be 3.00%; any shortfall is a gross-up or card-rate defect. Stripe's fee is QuotesDone's own cost, booked separately to 5000: 2.9% plus AED 1 on a domestic card, 3.9% plus AED 1 on others. Example: a AED 100,000 quote gives a AED 3,000 fee; the domestic Stripe cost is 0.029 x 3,000 + 1 = AED 88, leaving AED 2,912 in cash. Revenue is still recognised gross at AED 3,000.
items.note: 3.00% target; Stripe example arithmetic correct.

items.wording: How do we keep fraudsters with stolen cards from paying for unlocks?
items.answer: We screen every payment with Stripe Radar's default machine-learning rules and add custom rules on top. Sensible starting rules: request 3D Secure for new cards or elevated risk above a small amount (3DS usually shifts fraud-dispute liability to the issuer); review payments where card country and IP country differ and the customer is new; review disposable email domains combined with prepaid cards. Prefer review rules before block rules, keep allow rules minimal, and test a rule against the last six months of charges, or in 0% shadow mode, before activating it. A reveal whose payment is not confirmed is not revealed. I monitor dispute rate, fraud losses and refunds-as-fraud and report monthly. Changing live rules is a production change, so it goes through the change process with the IT engineer. If I suspect laundering or stolen-card fraud, I document facts, hold the money movement and hand the case to the CEO seat the same day, telling the customer only that the transaction is under review.

items.wording: At what stake does a shareholder count as the real owner we must record?
items.answer: A beneficial owner is a natural person who owns or controls 25% or more of the capital or voting rights, directly or indirectly through a chain of ownership, or who controls the entity by other means, such as the right to appoint or remove the majority of directors. If nobody meets the ownership test, the fallback is control by other means, and finally the senior managing official, so someone is always identified. Offshore holding layers do not break the chain; we follow it to the natural person. This is Cabinet Decision 109 of 2023. For QuotesDone, the founder is the sole beneficial owner. For suppliers, we collect owners of 25% or more and the manager named on the licence at onboarding so sanctions screening covers the real owners. Entities register within 60 days and record changes within 15 days.

items.wording: Do the anti-money-laundering rules treat a business like ours as a designated non-financial business?
items.answer: No, on the current analysis QuotesDone is not a designated non-financial business. Under Article 3 of Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025 the DNFBPs are gaming operators, real estate brokers, precious metals and stones dealers, lawyers and independent accountants for certain transactions, and trust and company service providers. We introduce buyers to suppliers and charge a fee through a licensed card processor; we hold no customer funds and do not transfer money. So we are not a DNFBP, financial institution or VASP, and the compulsory goAML registration, compliance officer and formal STR duty do not apply. Confidence is medium: the primary text was not fetched and the authority can add sectors. Re-check if we ever hold funds for others, release supplier payments, or list precious-metal or real-estate trades. The criminal offences and sanctions (TFS) duties apply to us regardless.

items.wording: We think a buyer may be laundering money. Should we let them know we are looking into it?
items.answer: No. We never tell the buyer, and never tell them a report is being considered or made. The message to them is neutral: the transaction is under review. Our practice is to document facts rather than conclusions, hold the related money movement, and hand the case to the CEO seat the same day. Whether to report to the authorities is a CEO decision and is recorded. Keep the evidence bundle for at least five years. Federal Decree-Law 10 of 2025 uses a should-have-known standard, so doing nothing about an obvious red flag is itself a risk.
items.note: Never tip off; neutral message; escalate to CEO, consistent with reference.

items.wording: When we hire, what end-of-service pay builds up in an employee's first five years?
items.answer: Under Article 51 of Federal Decree-Law 33 of 2021, an employee with at least one year of continuous service gets 21 days' basic wage for each of the first five years and 30 days for each additional year, on the last basic wage excluding allowances, pro rata for part years once the first year is complete, capped at two years' wage in total. Accounting-wise it is accrued monthly from the start date: basic monthly wage x 21/30 for each month of service in years one to five, even though nothing is payable before one year. Today we have no employees, so the liability is nil.

items.wording: Once we have staff, through what system must their salaries be paid?
items.answer: Through the Wage Protection System (WPS). Private-sector employers registered with the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MOHRE) pay wages electronically through WPS via approved agents, namely banks and exchange houses. A new WPS resolution, reported as effective 1 June 2026, requires wages to be processed through WPS or approved channels by the due date and at least 85% of wages due to be transferred on time. The exact due-day wording and penalty amounts were read only from secondary summaries and are not established here. When the first employee joins, I book a monthly payroll journal, pay net pay through the WPS agent matched to the salary information file acknowledgement, and book gratuity and leave accruals. Paying a person on a salary basis outside WPS is refused and escalated.

items.wording: Can the owner draw a salary from the company and count it as a deductible expense?
items.answer: A salary can be an expense of the company, but for Corporate Tax it is deductible only to the extent it matches market value for a service he actually renders and is wholly and exclusively for the business (Article 36 of the CT Law, since an owner is a connected person). It needs a written basis (role, amount, start date) and a market-value note before the first payment. A distribution of profit is equity, not an expense, and not deductible (Article 33(4)). Drawings are neither; they go to a receivable from the owner. An unlabelled payment is held as due from owner and raised to the CEO at month end.

items.wording: A tax question comes up that nobody here has seen before. How do you work it out?
items.answer: I follow a fixed sequence and show it in the answer. First, which tax it is: VAT, Corporate Tax, excise, or none (a DET licence fee or bank charge is not a tax). Second, our status on the date in question: VAT unregistered (below the AED 375,000 mandatory threshold), CT registered taxable person on the mainland, not a free zone person, not in a group, excise not applicable. Third, the governing provision, naming the article and the decree, regulation or decision number. Fourth, whether it is current: I check the MoF or FTA page for later amendments, and if I did not check this session I say so. Fifth, I apply it to our actual ledger figures and label the base (fees, not GMV). Then I give the conclusion first, then the provision, the figure, my confidence and anything not established. If a gap cannot be closed from a primary source, I say not established and escalate to the CEO rather than guess. If the answer changes a process, I update the tax calendar. Only UAE rules apply.
items.note: Gives the reasoning sequence including confidence and escalation.

items.wording: Customers in Sharjah say the portal will not load but every internal dashboard is green. What monitoring are we missing?
items.answer: Black-box synthetic probes from outside. Internal dashboards are white-box and only see what reaches the server, so a path failure for users in one place can leave them green. The probes should do HTTPS GETs of the home page, the customer and supplier portal login pages and a public health endpoint from outside Vercel and Supabase, checking status, a content marker and TLS validity, plus journey probes with a demo account. A probe failing twice in a row from two locations pages. Whether a Sharjah-specific vantage point exists is not established; the point is to add external probes from more than one location.
items.note: Black-box synthetic probes; internal metrics see only requests reaching server.

items.wording: How frequently do we test that an invited supplier can actually get through the launch flow?
items.answer: Every hour. The launchpath probe, which walks the invited-supplier and customer launch path read-only, runs hourly from resilience_ping (public.resilience_step). Read-only means it does not create real requests or messages for real people. It sits alongside the nightly full journey at 02:00 Dubai, which uses demo identities and Stripe in test mode only.

items.wording: What is our speed target for portal data loading, and do we judge it on the average?
items.answer: Page data must load in under 2.5 seconds, judged on the p95 (95th percentile), not the average. The mean hides the slow tail that one in twenty users actually feels. The hourly duty it_engineer.latency_slo computes p95 of the measured milliseconds per edge function, and for the home page, from the last 24 hours of runs. A function with at least 30 runs whose p95 exceeds its budget becomes a finding with blast customer_facing, raised to the owning seat.

items.wording: One slow call in a quiet function: is that already a latency finding?
items.answer: No. A finding needs at least 30 runs in the last 24 hours, and the function's p95 must exceed its budget (page data under 2.5 seconds). The 30-run floor exists precisely so that one slow cold start in a quiet function does not become a finding. The p95 is used rather than a single call or the mean. If the duty does fire, first check whether the slowness is the database (pg_stat_statements, a missing index), a cold start, or a provider call inside the request, before touching the budget.

items.wording: For a public-facing service, what are the core health signals a senior SRE looks at?
items.answer: The four golden signals. Latency: time to serve a request, measuring successes and failures separately because a fast error hides a slow success path. Traffic: demand in the system's own unit, such as RFQs, quotes, logins and outbound messages. Errors: explicit (5xx), implicit (a 200 with wrong content) and by policy (slower than the committed threshold). Saturation: how full the most constrained resource is, such as database connections, disk, edge-function CPU, outbox queue depth and provider rate limits. Saturation is the one most often missing and the one that predicts outages, so always ask which resource runs out first and in how many days. Add black-box synthetic probes that exercise the journeys from outside.

items.wording: Why is the silence detector designed to wait at least one tick before it complains?
items.answer: Because one missed tick is not evidence of a dead scheduler. The detector step itdetect runs every 15 minutes with a one-tick floor, because three missed ticks produced a false SCHEDULER DOWN page on 17 Sep 2026. The rule stays that a missing run is a finding in its own right and 'healthy' is never inferred from absence of errors; the floor only keeps a brief delay from raising a false page.

items.wording: If the overnight end-to-end run goes quiet, how long before it counts as missing?
items.answer: 26 hours. The nightly journey (.github/workflows/nightly-journey.yml, cron 0 22 * * *, which is 02:00 Dubai) is watched by heartbeat: if it has not reported for 26 hours, fn_it_duties raises a 'journey_heartbeat' finding. By comparison, the weekly readings count as missing after eight days, through fn_it_workflow_heartbeats. A missing run is a finding in its own right.

items.wording: How often does the background problem detector itself run?
items.answer: Every 15 minutes. The detector step itdetect runs on a 15-minute cadence with a one-tick floor, because three missed ticks produced a false SCHEDULER DOWN page on 17 Sep 2026. The step 'it', which raises what the detector wrote, runs on the same 15-minute cycle and must run after itdetect. A silent scheduler is detected by absence, so a missing run is a finding in its own right and we never infer 'healthy' from a lack of errors.

items.wording: Lots of OTP codes are being requested to numbers starting with the same digits. When is that a burst?
items.answer: The threshold in public.it_threshold is otp_burst_per_prefix_hour = 5, so more than a handful of code requests to one number prefix inside an hour is a burst. Related limits: otp_sms_per_ip_hour 10 and otp_signup_global_hour 60. The hourly otp duty detects it and the seat blocks the prefix itself for otp_block_hours, which is 24 hours. Per the pumping playbook, tighten the per-prefix limit and block the range first, then record the event with the cost measured from Twilio usage. Confirm with two independent signals, for example Twilio sends against verify conversion.

items.wording: We caught a number spamming login codes. For how long is it blocked?
items.answer: 24 hours. The threshold otp_block_hours in public.it_threshold is 24, so a blocked prefix or IP stays blocked for 24 hours. IT can lift a block earlier with fn_it_otp_unblock, and blocking is a door IT closes alone without asking anyone. The trigger thresholds that lead to a block are otp_burst_per_prefix_hour 5, otp_sms_per_ip_hour 10 and otp_signup_global_hour 60. The seat records the event with the cost measured from Twilio usage.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: At what point do we start warning before we hit a provider usage limit?
items.answer: At 80 percent. The usage duty runs hourly (fn_it_usage_watch) against the cap_* and floor_* rows and warns at cap_warn_ratio 0.8. Set values: cap_resend_emails_month 50000, cap_supabase_storage_bytes 100 GiB and db_disk_limit_bytes 18 GiB. cap_vercel_charges_month and floor_twilio_balance are empty, so no warning point is established for them. Supabase itself has no per-item budgets or threshold alerts, so for its spend-cap quotas the seat computes days-to-quota daily and raises a finding at a threshold the CEO sets.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: How many emails a month can we send on the current Resend plan before hitting the cap?
items.answer: The cap we have set is cap_resend_emails_month = 50000, so 50,000 emails a month, with the usage duty warning at 80 percent, which is 40,000 (0.8 x 50,000). What the sources do not establish is which Resend plan we are on or what the plan itself allows; the 50,000 is the cap value recorded in public.it_threshold, so read the plan limit from Resend before quoting it as a provider limit.

items.wording: In the Twilio log, two messages show different error states, "failed" and "undelivered". What does each mean?
items.answer: 'failed' means the message never left Twilio, so sending did not succeed. 'undelivered' means it was sent but the carrier or device did not accept it. Both, along with 'delivered' and 'read', are final statuses. 'read' is only reached where supported, namely WhatsApp and RCS.

items.wording: What share of WhatsApp messages failing should make IT open a finding?
items.answer: A failure rate above 5 percent: the threshold whatsapp_failure_rate_max is 0.05. It is judged only with at least whatsapp_min_final_7d = 10 final reports in 7 days. The hourly duty whatsapp_delivery (fn_it_whatsapp_delivery_health) runs it for customer_support, from Twilio delivery reports. A message with no final report after 24 hours is itself a finding.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: A WhatsApp send still has no delivered or failed status after 24 hours. What is probably wrong?
items.answer: Probably the status callback, not the delivery. A message stuck in 'sent' with no final status for 24 hours is itself a finding, because the callback may be broken. Check the webhook endpoint: a burst of 401/403 after an app-secret rotation means the edge function still holds the old secret, so update the function secret and verify with the next delivered status event. Meta retries failed deliveries for up to 36 hours, so duplicates are expected and processing must be keyed on message or status id. Also check the Meta token and scope; a persistent 403 cluster points to those.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: We just set up a new WhatsApp business number. How many different people can it message in a day at first?
items.answer: A new portfolio starts at 250 unique recipients of business-initiated messages per rolling 24 hours. That limit applies at the business portfolio level, not per phone number, so every number in the portfolio shares one allowance and one number can consume all of it. It rises to 2,000 by verifying the business, by partner verification, or by sending 2,000 delivered messages outside customer-service windows to unique recipients within 30 days using high-quality templates. After that it scales automatically (10,000, 100,000, unlimited) with consistently high quality and use of at least half the current limit in the last 7 days. Read the actual limit from the whatsapp_business_manager_messaging_limit field before each batch and pace campaigns under it, rather than assuming it.

items.wording: Without paying for an upgrade, what protection does Vercel give us against floods of traffic?
items.answer: Two things are free. First, the platform-wide Vercel Firewall applies automatic DDoS mitigation on every plan at no charge, blocking abnormal traffic volumes. Second, Attack Mode is free on all plans: browsers must pass a challenge while verified bots, search crawlers, webhook providers and our own functions and cron jobs pass unchallenged. Check that integrations calling the site are not blocked, and treat it as a response to a targeted attack, not a permanent setting. The WAF's project-level controls (custom rules, IP blocking, managed rulesets) exist, but the sources do not establish which of them our plan includes at no cost. The 40 rate-limit rules figure is stated for Pro projects. Read the project's current rules before saying what is deployed.

items.wording: For security monitoring, which events are we never allowed to skip in the logs?
items.answer: Per OWASP A09:2025 (Security Logging and Alerting Failures), always record authentication successes and failures, access-control failures, input and output validation failures, sensitive operations (user administration, use of encryption keys, imports and exports) and system events (startup, shutdown, errors, configuration changes). For us that means OTP issuance and verification, route and RLS denials, webhook signature failures, role and permission changes, secret creation, rotation and deletion, SQL applies, bulk exports and restores, supplier verification changes and admin actions. Each needs a timestamp, acting identity, source, action, target and outcome in structured form, plus an alert rule and an owner.

items.wording: In our two-sided platform, what access mistake would hurt us most?
items.answer: The costliest mistake is a break in pre-reveal anonymity or in supplier and buyer isolation. If a supplier's name, phone, email or licence number reaches any buyer-facing surface (API response, PDF, email, WhatsApp) before the paid reveal, the core of the service is gone. A close second is one supplier reading another supplier's quote or price, which breaks confidentiality. The usual technical causes are a table in an exposed schema with no RLS, since it is then readable and writable by any role holding a grant, a SECURITY DEFINER routine that anon can execute, or a service key near client code. Prevent it with grants plus policies on every table, ownership checks on every client-supplied id, server-side role checks, and pgTAP tests for denied cases as well as allowed ones.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: A developer says the bug is fixed and wants to close the ticket. What must be attached first?
items.answer: A check that fails if the cause returns (instr 573). A finding closed without such a check is not done, and the check must measure the same case the fault hit, not an easier one. For every closed critical or high fault the hourly postmortem duty also creates an incident record in public.it_incident with its root cause (playbook first, think() only for a new class) and a regression check. The check should be wired into CI or a scheduled duty, with an owner, due date and verifiable completion test on the postmortem action. Verification means the same query or probe that proved the problem now proves the fix, since 'no new errors' is not proof if traffic also dropped.

items.wording: The remediation playbook refers to a database function nobody can find. What happens?
items.answer: It fails loudly. fn_it_playbook_first finds the it_playbook row whose issue_prefix is the longest prefix of the issue key and has a remedy_routine, runs it once per occurrence, and logs agent_runs job 'playbook'. A playbook naming a missing routine raises an exception rather than silently passing. That makes the gap a visible failure, not a false pass. A remedy that keeps failing is a new incident: after a fixed number of failed attempts the playbook stops and escalates with evidence. The fix is to create or restore the routine, and the regression check should then fail if a playbook ever points at a missing routine again.

items.wording: Why should incident reviews avoid naming who caused the problem?
items.answer: Because blame makes people hide mistakes, and then the organisation cannot learn. A blameless postmortem looks for systemic weaknesses: what made the failure possible, why the safeguards did not catch it, and what delayed detection. Naming a person would stop at 'who' and never reach those causes. The reviewer checks that the data is complete, the impact is quantified, the causes go deep enough, and the actions are prioritised. Each action then gets an owning seat, a due date and a regression check that fails if the cause returns. At QuotesDone the owner is a seat, not a person, which fits the same principle.

items.wording: What is our most serious incident level and what triggers it?
items.answer: SEV1. It is a core journey (login, RFQ submission, quote submission, reveal) down for all or most users, confirmed or probable personal-data exposure, or money moving incorrectly. The commander is the CEO seat with it_engineer as operations lead, the founder is told at once, and updates continue at a fixed cadence until restored. SEV2 is a degraded journey for a segment, failing outbound email or WhatsApp, or stopped backups or restore drills. The ladder is QuotesDone's own convention, and severity is set from impact, not component.

items.wording: A function keeps answering "forbidden" to some callers. Is that IT's concern?
items.answer: Yes. Polite refusals are visible to IT (instruction 18): a system that says 'sorry, not allowed' with a 200-looking reply can hide a broken permission. fn_it_run_is_refusal marks a run as a refusal when counts.http is any 4xx, counts.signal is 'forbidden' or 'bad_secret', counts.authorised = '0', counts.forbidden > 0, or a matching 'fn:<agent>' run within 5 seconds returned 4xx. Unless the refusal is intended policy, it is a finding, because an unexpected 401/403 usually means an expired secret, a missing grant or a wrong key after rotation.

items.wording: How do we tell a refusal that is by design from one that signals a bug?
items.answer: Check it against public.it_refusal_policy using fn_it_refusal_is_policy(subject, counts). If the subject has a policy row whose reason_key is present in counts, the refusal is intended, for example a non-owner denied another supplier's quote, and it is not a finding. Any other refusal is a finding, because an unexpected 401/403 usually means an expired secret, a missing grant or a wrong key after rotation. Classify it from the structured fields (status code, signal), not from the reply text.

items.wording: The database feels slow. Where do we find which queries cost the most time?
items.answer: Use pg_stat_statements, which records every normalised statement keyed by queryid. Order by total_exec_time to see where the server's time really goes, since a cheap query called millions of times often outranks one slow report, then by mean_exec_time for individually slow statements. Check the Supabase inspect outliers command, compute cache hit percentage from shared_blks_hit and shared_blks_read, then run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a representative instance. Record findings by queryid, not SQL text. Run inspect commands with a statement timeout; that they are harmless under load is not established.

items.wording: How should we size the connection pool relative to Postgres max connections?
items.answer: Supabase suggests giving the Supavisor pool about 80% of max connections for general use, or about 40% when PostgREST is heavily used, because PostgREST, Auth, Storage and reserved roles also consume connections. The right figure depends on measured concurrent peak, not on a formula. For example, on a Small compute with 90 direct connections, 80% is 72 and 40% is 36. Which compute size we actually run is not established here. Keep the default max_connections. Edge and Vercel functions use transaction mode (port 6543), while migrations, dumps and advisory-lock holders use session mode or a direct connection. When connections run out, first look for a caller opening direct or session connections from a serverless function, and for idle-in-transaction sessions, before paying for more compute.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: How should we report that the disk is filling, so someone acts on it?
items.answer: Report it as days to the limit, with the arithmetic shown, and act on it ourselves. Take the finite limit from configuration (db_disk_limit_bytes is 18 GiB), take a daily reading, fit a simple linear trend over the last few weeks, and compute remaining headroom divided by daily growth. Usage warnings start at 80% (cap_warn_ratio 0.8), which is 14.4 GiB of 18 GiB. Raise a ticket when days-to-limit falls below the time needed to act (an upgrade or a table clean-up), and an incident if it falls below a few days. The report states the reading, the limit, the trend and the date, so the CEO seat sees the numbers behind any upgrade request. IT does not merely notify. It records what it did and the evidence.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: Is a copy in Supabase alone enough for our backups?
items.answer: No. Supabase's managed backups and PITR are copy 2 on the same provider as production. Daily backups are kept 7 days on Pro, 14 on Team and 30 on Enterprise, and they do not contain Storage objects (only metadata rows), so supplier documents, drawings and PDFs need their own copy. Our rule is that backups go to both Supabase and Dropbox, incrementally. The nightly table export to Dropbox is the different-provider, off-site copy for the 3-2-1 rule. Whether the Dropbox copy is protected against deletion by the same automation token is not established, and the seat must check that before reporting the rule as met. Which Supabase plan we are on and whether PITR is enabled are not established here. Any copy counts only once a restore drill has proved it.

items.wording: How stale can the latest table export get before IT treats it as a problem?
items.answer: Two days. The threshold public.it_threshold restore_export_max_age_days is 2, so a latest table export older than 2 days is a problem. The daily backup_gap duty also raises every open gap source in the backup registry, and export_incremental_min_bytes is 64 MiB, so an incremental export below that size is also suspect. A restore drill that fails is a severity-2 finding owned by it_engineer with a fix date, and the backup it tested is treated as not existing until a re-drill passes. Two consecutive misses of the drill cadence are themselves reported.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: On our current Supabase plan, how far back do the automatic daily backups go?
items.answer: It depends on the plan, and the sources do not say which plan we are on, so read it from the dashboard. Supabase retains daily backups for 7 days on Pro, 14 days on Team and 30 days on Enterprise. Daily backups do not contain Storage objects, and after restoring one the custom database role passwords must be reset. If PITR is enabled, its recovery windows are sold at 7, 14 or 28 days.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: With point-in-time recovery enabled, how much data could we lose in the worst case?
items.answer: About two minutes in the worst case. With PITR, Supabase archives WAL every two minutes, so the worst-case recovery point is about two minutes, with restore granularity of seconds. With daily backups only, the loss can be up to a day. Caveats: PITR is an add-on needing at least the Small compute add-on, so read from the dashboard whether it is enabled on production rather than assuming. Storage objects are not in database backups even with PITR, and the approved RPO is a CEO-seat decision, so the target is not established.

items.wording: Which bounce rate tells us our sending reputation is in trouble?
items.answer: Our threshold is sender_bounce_rate_max = 0.02, so a bounce rate above 2 percent raises a finding. It is judged only with at least sender_min_sends_7d = 20 sends in 7 days, so a tiny sample cannot raise a false alarm. The complaint threshold is sender_complaint_rate_max 0.003 (0.3 percent). Separately, Gmail's spam rate should stay below 0.3 percent, with a best-practice target below 0.10 percent; we raise a finding if it approaches 0.1 percent.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: The Spamhaus lookup came back with 127.255.255.254. Are we on a blocklist?
items.answer: No. 127.255.255.254 is an error, not a listing. Spamhaus refuses queries from public resolvers (Google, Cloudflare, Quad9) and answers with that code. A real listing is an answer in 127.0.0.x (127.0.0.2 SBL, 127.0.0.3 CSS, 127.0.0.4 XBL, 127.0.0.10-11 PBL), and NXDOMAIN means not listed. So the check has not yet told us anything; repeat the lookup from a resolver that is not one of those public ones.

items.wording: Can we add a second SPF TXT record for a new email provider?
items.answer: Not as a second record. A domain must publish only one SPF record; multiple records produce a permanent error that receivers treat as a failed check. Add the new provider to the existing record, usually with an include, within the limit of 10 DNS lookups (include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect count, and nested includes too). Exceeding 10 is also a permanent error, and void lookups should stay at two, so retire stale includes. Then re-check the record after the provider change; the DNS duty counts lookups recursively and flags duplicates.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: What has to be true for an email to pass DMARC?
items.answer: DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes and the authenticated domain aligns with the domain in the visible From header (RFC5322.From). Both conditions are needed: authentication alone is not enough. Under relaxed alignment the organisational domains must match, so mail.quotesdone.ae aligns with quotesdone.ae. Strict alignment needs an exact match of the full domain name. This is why SPF alone does not stop From spoofing, since SPF checks the envelope sender domain. The published policy (p=none, quarantine or reject, with pct and rua reporting) then decides what receivers do with failing mail.

items.wording: From what daily sending volume does Gmail insist on a DMARC record?
items.answer: From 5,000 or more messages a day to Gmail accounts. Those senders must additionally publish DMARC, have the From domain align with the SPF or DKIM domain, and support one-click unsubscribe. The floor for all senders is SPF or DKIM, valid forward and reverse DNS, TLS, RFC 5322 formatting, and a spam rate below 0.3% (target below 0.10%). QuotesDone is below the 5,000 threshold today, but campaigns, supplier recruitment and digests can cross it quickly. We should therefore run both SPF and DKIM and keep DMARC aligned on every sending domain, and raise a finding if the spam rate approaches 0.1%.

items.wording: Twilio charges jumped this week. How big a jump does IT treat as an anomaly?
items.answer: Provider spend is judged daily. It is an anomaly at twice its own baseline (spend_anomaly_multiple 2), with a floor of AED 20 (spend_floor_aed 20) so tiny amounts never page. A Twilio jump therefore counts only if the day's spend is at least double Twilio's own normal and above that floor. A jump like this is also a prompt to check for SMS pumping: look at OTP sends per prefix, with the thresholds otp_burst_per_prefix_hour 5, otp_sms_per_ip_hour 10 and otp_signup_global_hour 60. Block the abusive prefix immediately and record the cost from Twilio usage. The floor_twilio_balance threshold is empty, so it is not established.
items.note: States 2x baseline (multiple 2) with AED 20 floor; AED 20 is spend_floor_aed 20 from the reference, so the CHECK figure is correct; extra detail does not contradict.

items.wording: If we hit a Supabase quota while the spend cap is on, what does the platform do?
items.answer: With the spend cap on, once a quota is exceeded further usage of that item is disallowed until the next billing cycle. That protects against runaway cost but restricts service, so the failure mode is an outage, not a bill. Covered items include disk size, egress, Edge Function invocations, logs, monthly active users, Realtime and storage image transformations; compute, PITR, read replicas and log drains are not covered. There are no per-item budgets or threshold alerts, so the seat computes days-to-quota daily from its own usage readings and treats a sudden jump in invocations or egress first as a possible attack or loop.

items.wording: We generated a new API key. When can we say the rotation is complete?
items.answer: Not when the key is generated or the secret is set; that is only one step. Rotation is complete when the provider shows the new key in use and the old key's request count is zero, with a real authenticated call or signed event from every consumer recorded as evidence. Then revoke the old key, verify a call with it now fails, and record the timestamps, consumers and proofs in it_credential_rotation. For Vercel sensitive values, which cannot be read back, success is an authenticated call from the new deployment. For WhatsApp, send a test message through the real outbox, then invalidate the old token. If any consumer cannot be verified, stop and hand off.
missing: the old one no longer works
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: Why bother changing secrets on a schedule if none has leaked?
items.answer: Because rotation is what limits the damage of a leak nobody has noticed. Rotating regularly means a stolen secret works only briefly; frequency depends on the secret's function, from minutes for session keys to years for hardware-bound ones, while user credentials are rotated only on suspected compromise. Our audit found the rotation duty running but zero rotations ever recorded, so the lifecycle was monitored in name only until a rotation is performed and proved end to end. Every credential should have an owner, a last-rotated date and a proof of rotation. A secret that was ever pushed must be assumed copied.

items.wording: Which outside services do we check for outages every hour?
items.answer: The hourly provider_status duty (fn_it_provider_watch) reads the status pages of Stripe, Resend, Twilio, Vercel, Supabase and Dropbox, plus the Vercel firewall. OpenRouter has its own hourly meter step. A provider outage opens an external cause (it_integration_external_cause), so our own findings that it caused are attributed to it rather than chased. The hourly launchpath probe is different: it walks our own invited-supplier and customer launch path read-only, so it is not an outside-service check.

items.wording: Someone changed a database function directly in production. How would we find out?
items.answer: The deploy-drift guard. fn_it_change_watch reads public.it_change_revision for revisions first seen in the last 30 days whose verdict is not on_main or merged_pr. A revision still 'pending' or 'open_pr' gets 2 hours of grace, because the estate applies before it merges. A change is settled only when every change it made, recorded in public.routine_change_log with application_name 'qd-apply <sha> ...', was re-applied from a reviewed revision or accepted in it_change_acceptance. Anything else is an unauthorised change and becomes a finding. The project-parity.yml workflow exists so that drift cannot silently return.

items.wording: When the drift guard first compared production to the repo, how much mismatch did it find?
items.answer: On 2026-08-10 the first count found 602 objects of drift. Of those, 127 were cron jobs and 464 were SECURITY DEFINER functions executable by anon on one side. That accounts for 591, leaving 11 objects whose type the source does not break down. The project-parity.yml workflow was created so that drift cannot silently return. Related trap: applying an old file resurrects a superseded routine, because the highest MANIFEST key is canonical, not the file you applied.

items.wording: A frontend release broke sign-in. What is the quickest way to undo it?
items.answer: Use Vercel Instant Rollback. It points the production domains back to a previous production deployment instantly, with no rebuild, and is almost always faster and safer than fixing forward. Pick the last good production deployment (Pro and Enterprise can pick any eligible one; Hobby only the immediately previous one), then verify with the synthetic probes that sign-in works and the error rate returns to its pre-deploy baseline. Cautions: the database is not rolled back, so the old frontend must work against any new schema; cron jobs revert to that deployment's definition; and environment variable changes since then are not applied. The trap is that after a rollback Vercel stops auto-assigning production domains, so a merged fix will not go live until you promote a deployment (Undo Rollback or vercel promote). Record the rollback, reason and undo in the incident timeline, then diagnose and ship the fix as a Normal change with the missed test added.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: At what time does the full overnight customer journey test start?
items.answer: At 02:00 Dubai time. The workflow .github/workflows/nightly-journey.yml runs on cron '0 22 * * *' (that is UTC, which equals 02:00 in Dubai). It drives scripts/e2e/run.mjs on demo identities at reserved addresses, Stripe in test mode only, tears down every row by its tag, and hands the result to fn_it_journey_ingest. If it has not reported for 26 hours, a journey_heartbeat finding is raised.

items.wording: Right after a deploy, what does the automatic smoke test check?
items.answer: After every merge to main whose edge-function deploy succeeded, the post-deploy smoke (it-post-deploy-smoke.yml) waits for Vercel's production deployment of the same commit and runs a short journey: sign in, portal overview, one request, one quote, and the comparison PDF in English and Arabic. It then purges what it created and sends the result with the changed files to fn_it_smoke_ingest. A failed step goes to the seat owning most of the changed files. Measured 28 Sep: the last smoke was 24 Sep, with an open finding duty:smoke:run:fixture_setup_failed, so it needs attention.
missing: comparison PDF in en and ar
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: How would we spot test data leaking into real reports?
items.answer: The daily data_quality duty (it_engineer.data_quality) looks for it. It checks for demo rows crossing into real parties, orphans, and transaction-quote mismatches, and raises each to the owning seat. Demo fixtures follow a fixed convention: names starting 'ZZ DEMO' and addresses on example.invalid. So any real-party row or real number that carries those markers is test data leaking in. The same convention lets the failure-cluster logic exclude demo fixtures. The nightly journey also uses demo identities with Stripe in test mode only and tears down every row by its tag, so a surviving tagged row is a signal as well.

items.wording: How do we know whether a seat's knowledge is getting worse?
items.answer: By running each seat's evaluation set on a schedule and after any change to the pack, the retrieval function or the model. Store per-question results with the pack version so a drop can be traced to a cause. Measure retrieval hit rate, context precision and recall, and faithfulness and relevancy. Raise a finding to the owning seat when the pass rate falls below its last accepted baseline, or when any previously passing question now fails. Never fix a drop by editing the expected ids to match what was retrieved, because that would certify the gap. No absolute pass-rate target is established, since the CEO seat sets it. A quarterly refresh also re-reviews old or low-confidence entries.

items.wording: The knowledge was verified once. Why re-check it every quarter?
items.answer: Because knowledge ages. Laws gain executive regulations, platform limits and prices change, standards publish new versions (OWASP Top 10 moved to a 2025 edition and ASVS to 5.0.0 in 2025), and entries marked 'not established' may become established. Each quarter one refresh task per seat is opened with the entries due: those whose as_of date is old, those of low or medium confidence, those containing 'not established', and those whose sources failed the link check. A reviewed entry gets a new as_of date and changed content or a 'reviewed, unchanged' record, and the seat's evaluation set is re-run against its baseline.

items.wording: How do we tell a model-call loop from normal busy traffic?
items.answer: By attribution and by comparison with the consumer's own history. Every model call is attributed to a consumer in public.it_model_consumer, and the hourly model_spend duty raises findings to the owning seat for three things: an unlisted consumer, a loop, and a repeated uncached call. A loop is defined as 5x the consumer's usual hour, so it is judged against that consumer's own baseline, not against site traffic. Daily provider spend is also watched, with an anomaly at twice its own baseline and a floor of AED 20. Idle internal spend has a founder ceiling of about USD 1-2 per day. Busy traffic raises usage in proportion across consumers, whereas a loop shows one consumer far above its own hour.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: What is the most we may spend per day on models when no customer is using the platform?
items.answer: About USD 1-2 per day. That is the founder's ceiling for idle internal spend (instr 986), meaning model spend when nothing customer-driven is happening. It is an approximate ceiling, not an exact cap. It is enforced by the hourly model_spend duty, which attributes every call to a consumer and flags unlisted consumers, loops at 5x the usual hour and repeated uncached calls. The daily provider-spend duty adds an anomaly flag at twice baseline with an AED 20 floor. The doctrine behind it is that about 95% of internal operation is deterministic code and only about 5% uses a model.
items.note: States about USD 1-2 per day as the founder's idle internal spend ceiling; AED 20 matches the reference floor, no contradiction.

items.wording: In the monthly restore test, how many rows are compared against live?
items.answer: 50 rows. The monthly restore_table drill takes 50 rows of one table page from the newest export and compares them in a scratch schema. The monthly files drill separately restores 5 random files (restore_sample_files). Both run every 30 days under the it_duty_schedule. The last recorded drills were 14 Sep (supplier_dues page, failed) and 15 Sep (quotes page, passed). The separate proposed weekly drill, which compares row counts and checksums, is awaiting CEO-seat approval and is not the monthly test.

items.wording: Our backups run every night. Why also test restoring them?
items.answer: Because a backup is a claim until a restore proves it. The audit found the table restore drill had run only twice, the last on 15 September with one of the two failing, and no drill had ever restored the whole database. Supabase's limits also make drills necessary: daily backups do not contain Storage objects, the project is inaccessible during a restore for a size-dependent time, and custom role passwords must be reset after a daily-backup restore. Proposed cadence, pending CEO approval: weekly table restore, monthly Storage spot-check, quarterly full rehearsal into a separate project. A failed drill is a severity-2 finding.
missing: never been restored is an assumption
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: Which platform accounts does the monthly access review cover?
items.answer: GitHub, Vercel, Stripe and Dropbox. The access duty runs every 30 days, and each holder is reconfirmed within access_reconfirm_days 90. The monthly review is only the safety net. When a person, seat or integration no longer needs access, it is removed the same day on every console, which also includes Supabase, Twilio, Meta, Resend and the registrar, with tokens revoked, shared secrets rotated and evidence recorded. Supabase members are separately covered by the weekly readings.

items.wording: Will the monthly dependency check update packages automatically?
items.answer: No. The monthly dependency security scan and patches run on weekly readings plus fn_it_dependency_ingest, and produce at most one lockfile-only pull request for independent review, which is never auto-merged. Security-update PRs go through the normal review and CI path like any code change, because even a patch release can be compromised. Updates go in small batches with CI and a preview deploy so a bad one can be reverted alone, and CI installs with npm ci so the lockfile is exactly what gets built. Each review is recorded: the dependency, the advisory, the decision and the date.

items.wording: A scary CVE was published for a library. What is the first thing to establish?
items.answer: First establish whether the vulnerable package or version is actually deployed, checking the lockfile, the Deno import map or the Supabase/Postgres version. If it is not, close the advisory as not affected and record the evidence. If it is deployed, go on in order: is the vulnerable code path reachable from an internet-facing surface (portal, edge function, webhook); the severity, using the CVSS score labelled with its nomenclature (usually CVSS-B, which reflects severity, not risk to us); and the likelihood, using the EPSS score and whether active exploitation is reported. Reachable and (Critical or actively exploited) means patch or mitigate now and verify by re-running the probe; reachable High goes in the next deploy; unreachable or Low is batched with routine updates. Target windows in days are a CEO decision and are not yet established, so until then we report the age of every open advisory.

items.wording: When does the TLS certificate on quotesdone.ae run out?
items.answer: The quotesdone.ae TLS certificate expires on 2026-11-09, as measured on 28 Sep 2026 in public.it_expiry (quotesdone.com's is 2026-11-08). fn_it_renewal_watch warns at 60 and 30 days. Vercel renews both automatically, so a certificate inside 30 days of expiry means the renewal did not happen and is a finding. The domain registrations are separate: quotesdone.ae 2027-06-07 and quotesdone.com 2027-06-08.

items.wording: When must the company trade licence be renewed?
items.answer: The trade licence (DET Dubai Trader License no. 1633275, issued 25 Jun 2026) expires 24 Jun 2027, and renewal is a company task due then; the renewal watch lists it for 2027-06-24, with warnings at 60 and 30 days via fn_it_renewal_watch over public.it_expiry. Supplier trade-licence expiry is a different duty, owned by sales_engineer.

items.wording: Apart from restores, access reviews and renewals, what else does IT do every month?
items.answer: Two more monthly duties are named: the dependency security scan and patches (weekly readings plus fn_it_dependency_ingest, at most one lockfile-only PR for independent review, never auto-merged), and a performance review every month. The performance review is read against the job-description KPIs: 99.9% uptime or better, error rate, p95 latency with page data loading under 2.5 seconds, MTTD and MTTR, backups current and restores passing, inbox deliverability, findings open more than 24 hours, and founder emails per week (fewer is better). Targets the CEO seat has not approved are reported as measured value plus 'target not established'.

items.wording: The production database is gone. What is the very first step?
items.answer: Declare the incident. Name the surface that is down (here the Supabase project), since when, and the customer impact, and open the incident record with a start time, severity, affected journeys and a named commander. Second comes the freeze: pause pg_cron jobs that send or write, pause campaigns, and show the maintenance message if data integrity is in doubt. Only then comes the recovery, restoring PITR or the latest backup into a new project first, and never rehearsing over production. Remember that Storage objects are not in database backups, and that custom role passwords must be reset after a daily-backup restore. Record the timeline and the achieved RPO and RTO.

items.wording: In the quarterly review, what else besides disaster recovery is covered?
items.answer: Besides the disaster-recovery exercise, the quarterly review covers a capacity and cost review (headroom stated as days to the limit, provider bills against plan) and a check that the code is healthy and organised, the auditor-readable structure rule. The quarterly knowledge refresh is also wired as a duty. The DR exercise, the capacity and cost review and the code-health check must each run as a scheduled duty with a recorded result; until one does, its absence is an open finding, not a pass. The full restore rehearsal is also quarterly.

items.wording: Which quarterly check looks at the code base itself?
items.answer: The quarterly code-health check, which verifies that the code is healthy and organised under the auditor-readable structure rule. It is one of the three quarterly reviews alongside the disaster-recovery exercise and the capacity and cost review. It must run as a scheduled duty with a recorded result; until it does, its absence is an open finding, not a pass.

items.wording: Does IT need permission before rolling back a release or rotating a key?
items.answer: No. The IT seat decides alone, without asking anyone, any technical fix, rollback, retry, failover or key rotation, and any door it closes. It must not wait for approval to restore service, and it records every action with the evidence that it worked. What it does not take alone is anything involving money, refunds or destructive production changes. Cautions: a Vercel rollback does not revert database changes or cron configuration, and it turns off automatic production assignment until you promote or undo. A key rotation is complete only when the new key is proved by a successful call, and the old key's request count is zero.

items.wording: When is it right for IT to email the founder directly?
items.answer: Rarely. The founder is emailed only for a genuinely new bug class, once, with what was already done, and never for a daily storm of alerts. The test runs in order: if there is a playbook, run it and verify; if the class has been seen before in incident memory, it is not new and is not emailed; if it hurts customers, suppliers or money, tell the CEO seat with evidence; only then, if it is a genuinely new bug class, email the founder. An alert or email is a record of what the seat did, never a hand-off asking him to solve it. Technical items are never a decision for the founder, and the severity ladder's 'founder told at once' wording is overridden by the settled rule that incidents are reported to the CEO seat.

items.wording: A fault is hurting customers. Who must IT inform?
items.answer: The CEO seat, with evidence, because the fault hurts customers. A customer-visible fault is also a trigger to declare an incident, opening one record with a named commander. IT is the commander and operations lead for technical incidents. The CEO seat commands where there is business, legal or money impact, and decides what reaches the founder. Other seats are informed as needed: customer_support communicates to affected customers and suppliers, and the accountant acts when payments are affected. The founder is not the escalation path unless it is a genuinely new bug class, and then by one email stating what was already done. Link all related findings to the one incident.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: How much downtime per month does a 99.9% uptime target allow?
items.answer: 43.2 minutes in a 30-day month. The downtime budget is 0.1% of the window, so 0.1% of 30 days (43,200 minutes) is 43.2 minutes. In a 28-day window it is about 40.3 minutes. The older proposed 99.5% would have allowed 3.6 hours in 30 days, five times more. The 99.9% figure is the SLO the job description sets for every core journey and it supersedes the 99.5%.

items.wording: On 28 September, how many open findings were past 24 hours?
items.answer: 30 of the 34 open findings. Measured on 28 Sep 2026 in public.it_engineer_finding, 34 findings were open and 30 had been open for more than 24 hours. That KPI is therefore failing. Most of the old ones are handoffs owned by other seats (handoff_sla, sender templates, smoke fixture), so closing them means driving the owning seat to resolve them, not re-raising them.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: If we promise 99.5% success over 28 days, how much failure can we afford?
items.answer: A 99.5% objective over 28 days allows 0.5% of eligible requests to fail. In time terms, 28 days is 40,320 minutes and 0.5% of that is about 201.6 minutes (3.4 hours). However, our actual SLO for every core journey is 99.9%, set by the job description, which supersedes the older proposed 99.5%. That allows only about 40.3 minutes in 28 days. We should not quote an error-budget percentage against a target that has not been approved. When reporting, give consumed budget, remaining budget and the incident or change that consumed it.

items.wording: Customer data was exposed. Which UAE law sets our duties?
items.answer: The federal Personal Data Protection Law, Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 (PDPL), is our baseline because QuotesDone is a Dubai mainland company. Article 9, as reported by secondary legal sources, requires reporting the breach to the UAE Data Office immediately on becoming aware, with nature, causes, approximate numbers, the DPO's details, likely effects and corrective measures, and notifying affected data subjects. The Executive Regulations are not confirmed published, so no statutory deadline in hours or days is established; we act immediately. The CEO seat decides notification with legal advice. This is operational guidance, not legal advice.

items.wording: Before wiring in a new payment provider, what security step comes first?
items.answer: A threat model, before any code. Draw the data flow (actors, processes, data stores and trust boundaries such as browser to edge function, and platform to Stripe), answer the four questions (what are we working on, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, did we do a good enough job), and walk each element through STRIDE. Every change that adds a trust boundary, an external integration or a new way to move money carries a short STRIDE table in its PR, each threat with a mitigation, an owner and a test; a threat without a mitigation blocks the merge.

items.wording: An alert fired at night and nobody knew what to do. What was missing?
items.answer: A runbook. Every alert must link to one with the same sections: what the alert means and its customer impact, how to confirm it is real (the exact query or probe), mitigations in order of safety (roll back, flag off, pause a sender), how to verify recovery, who else must be told, and where to record the incident. The it_engineer seat is the on-call engineer and acts without waiting for the founder, but it cannot act on an alert it has no steps for. An alert with no runbook, or whose runbook proved wrong, produces a postmortem action to write or fix the runbook. An alert with no named surface is itself a defect.
items.note: Runbook named but not that alerts without one should not page

items.wording: How can we be sure our recovery works without waiting for a real failure?
items.answer: By rehearsing it on a schedule. Restore drills run every 30 days (restore for files, restore_table for a table), plus a quarterly full restore rehearsal into a separate non-production project, never over production, measuring RTO and achieved RPO. A game day happens once a quarter, with a written hypothesis and result, run only in the sandbox or against synthetic ZZ DEMO data. Candidate experiments are the email provider returning errors, the AI gateway timing out, a skipped cron tick, and a restore to a scratch project. A failed hypothesis becomes a fix with a regression check, and nothing is injected into production traffic with real customers. Runbooks are tested in these drills. If a DR exercise has no scheduled duty with a recorded result, its absence is an open finding, not a pass.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: Is a text-message code good enough to protect our Stripe and GitHub admin logins?
items.answer: No. SMS and voice codes are the weakest second factor because of SIM swap and interception. CISA's guidance is that phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 security keys or passkeys) is strongest, and app push should use number matching. Apply this to every admin console that controls the company (Stripe, GitHub, Supabase, Vercel, registrar and DNS, email, Meta, Twilio, Resend). Combine it with least privilege: minimal owners, scoped keys such as Stripe restricted keys and separate test and live, and written break-glass access. The seat keeps a register of each console with its MFA method and owners, reviews it quarterly, and treats any console without MFA or with an unexplained owner as an open security finding.

items.wording: We are a small team. Which security baseline should we implement first?
items.answer: Start with CIS Controls v8 Implementation Group 1: 56 safeguards of essential cyber hygiene meant for small organisations. Map each safeguard to the duty, check or document that proves it, and report the unmapped ones as the security backlog, never as 'compliant'. Within that, begin with the admin consoles: phishing-resistant MFA and least privilege everywhere, and sensitive environment variables in Vercel for every provider secret. The UAE Information Assurance Regulation is not mandatory for us (private mainland company, not designated critical), so treat it as a voluntary benchmark alongside OWASP, ASVS and NIST CSF. Security headers and a nonce-based CSP follow, introduced first in Report-Only mode.

items.wording: A large buyer's procurement team asks for our SOC 2 report. What do we say?
items.answer: Tell them the truth: QuotesDone holds neither SOC 2 nor ISO/IEC 27001, and does not need either before launch, so we never claim a certification we do not hold. What we can offer is vendor evidence: the main platforms we run on publish SOC 2 or ISO 27001 reports through their trust centres, and we keep a vendor-assurance register (vendor, report, period, date checked). The current report types and dates for each of our vendors are not verified, so they must be read from each trust page before we quote them. We can also answer a questionnaire by mapping our real controls, such as access controls and RLS, backups and restore drills, and incident response. A Type II report is the one buyers usually ask for.
items.note: All rubric points made; consistent with reference.

items.wording: Which kind of load test tells us the most traffic we can handle?
items.answer: A breakpoint test. It ramps load until something fails, which finds the ceiling. A stress test goes above normal to see how the system degrades, while smoke, average-load, spike and soak tests answer other questions. Each test states its goal, traffic model, pass/fail thresholds (for example p95 under the SLO and error rate under 1%) and what is watched: database connections and CPU, edge-function duration and errors, and provider rate limits. Run it against the sandbox or synthetic ZZ DEMO data, never real users or real sends. Every test ends with a written capacity number and the first component to fail.

items.wording: How can we follow one buyer's inquiry through every service in the logs?
items.answer: Carry one trace or correlation id through every hop. The practical target is that one inquiry can be followed from the web request through the edge functions, the database routines and the outbound email or WhatsApp send by a single id. Every new edge function logs structured JSON carrying the request's trace or correlation id and an error code, never secrets or personal data. In OpenTelemetry terms the trace id travels in the W3C traceparent header and logs that carry it tie to the spans. In Supabase, start in the Logs Explorer for the service that owns the symptom; retention is limited and depends on the plan.

items.wording: What does a domain need to qualify for the HSTS preload list?
items.answer: The HSTS preload list requires a max-age of at least one year (31536000 seconds), the includeSubDomains directive and the preload directive, and the site must serve HTTPS. Removal is slow, so every subdomain must serve HTTPS before preloading. Any HSTS, CAA or DNS change goes through a PR with the before and after records.

items.wording: How should an emergency stop for a mass campaign send work?
items.answer: Through a kill switch built beforehand. Bulk campaign sends, paid ad auto-spend, the model runtime and the email and WhatsApp outboxes each need an ops toggle that is readable at runtime, flips without a deploy, fails safe (off) when unreadable, and has been exercised in a game day. In an emergency we ship the smallest reversible change first (flag off, pause the sender or the cron job), and the proper fix follows later as a Normal change, with the emergency change reviewed in the postmortem. Every flag has an owner, a kind and a removal date, and every temporary change is written into the incident record so it is reversed at closure. Auto-remediation playbooks likewise have a kill switch the CEO seat can turn off without a deploy.
